stem: A frequency distribution of marks scored by 60 students has five class intervals. Four of the five class counts are known. Class 0-10 has 5 students, class 20-30 has 18, class 30-40 has 14, and class 40-50 has 7. The frequency of class 10-20 is missing. What is the missing frequency?

per_option_rationale.rationale: The student reads the frequency of class 20-30 as 17 instead of 18, slipping by one unit, and computes 60 - (5 + 17 + 14 + 7) = 17.
Sum of known frequencies = 5 + 18 + 14 + 7 = 44. Missing frequency = 60 - 44 = 16.
The student assumes equal distribution across all 5 classes: 60 / 5 = 12, ignoring the known frequencies entirely.
The student computes the sum of the four known frequencies (44) and reports that sum as the answer instead of subtracting from the total.

explanation: The total frequency is 60. The sum of the four known frequencies is 5 + 18 + 14 + 7 = 44. The missing frequency is 60 - 44 = 16.

explanation_sections.punchline: All frequencies must sum to the total. Known sum = 5+18+14+7 = 44. Missing = 60-44 = 16.
explanation_sections.approach: Apply the closure property: every frequency distribution must satisfy Sum(all f_i) = N. With one unknown, the missing frequency = N - Sum(known f_i). Add the four known values (5+18+14+7 = 44) then subtract from 60. The trap in option 4 is reporting the sum 44 instead of computing 60-44.
explanation_sections.lesson: One-missing-frequency problems have a single arithmetic step: total minus known sum. They test whether a student applies the constraint Sum = N or confuses the intermediate sum (44) with the answer.
explanation_sections.timing: 40 seconds. Add 5+18=23, 23+14=37, 37+7=44 in 15 seconds. 60-44=16 in 5 seconds. Done.
